How can value estimates grow forever when every reward is zero?

Part 5. Three useful ideas can form a feedback loop. A shared formula changes several predictions at once. Bootstrapping turns a prediction into a target. Sampling away from the target policy's state distribution can leave the inflated prediction without enough correction. The deadly triad names this risk, not an inevitable outcome.

Throughout, StS_tSt​ and AtA_tAt​ are the state and action at step ttt, and Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ is the reward after that action. The discount is 0≤γ<10\leq\gamma<10≤γ<1, and αt>0\alpha_t>0αt​>0 is a learning rate. A superscript +++ marks an updated quantity. Here, ttt is a step index, not an exponent. Let's calculate one loop that keeps growing, then compare three settings where learning is stable under specific assumptions. Van Hasselt et al., §2.

Reading goal: work out why the weight grows by 8% per replay, then identify exactly which assumption each stable pair restores.

Three pressures, one loopTwo states, one weightMatch the prediction distributionKeep the labels fixedSeparate the table entriesSlow the target feedbackCheck estimates beside rewards

Three pressures, one loop

If you wait for an episode to end, you delay learning. If you keep a table for every observation, you run out of memory. And if you require data from exactly the policy you're evaluating, you limit what you can reuse. Bootstrapping, function approximation and off-policy learning address those three problems.

Read the loop clockwise: raising one prediction also raises the successor prediction that shares its weights. That successor supplies the next target, so the sampled updates raise the original prediction again. With too little corrective sampling, this loop can keep growing. We'll calculate the multiplier in the next section. The missing correction is what matters here. Raising a successor is harmless if later data correct it, but if replay never trains there, the inflated target can stay in place. Van Hasselt et al., §2.

Each of the three pairs below is stable in a specific setting with its own assumptions. That doesn't give us a universal rule that any pair is safe or that every triple diverges.

Two states, one weight

Every reward is zero, so both true values are zero. The subscripts 1 and 2 label states. We use a scalar weight www and scalar feature ϕ(s)\phi(s)ϕ(s) to produce estimates vw(s1)=wv_w(s_1)=wvw​(s1​)=w and vw(s2)=2wv_w(s_2)=2wvw​(s2​)=2w, from fixed features ϕ(s1)=1\phi(s_1)=1ϕ(s1​)=1 and ϕ(s2)=2\phi(s_2)=2ϕ(s2​)=2.

δ=0+γ(2w)−w=(2γ−1)w,w+=w+αδϕ(s1)=[1+α(2γ−1)]w.\begin{aligned} \delta&=0+\gamma(2w)-w=(2\gamma-1)w,\\ w^+&=w+\alpha\delta\phi(s_1)=[1+\alpha(2\gamma-1)]w. \end{aligned} δw+​=0+γ(2w)−w=(2γ−1)w,=w+αδϕ(s1​)=[1+α(2γ−1)]w.​

Here the mismatch is state sampling, not action choice. Target-policy trajectories eventually stay at s2s_2s2​, but replay never starts there. This construction violates state coverage, so it isn't a counterexample to the pair guarantees below. Two-state construction.

Match the prediction distribution

The replay example left out the state that needed correction. What happens if we sample from the fixed policy's own trajectories while keeping approximation and bootstrapping? This changes the weighting used in the stability argument. For feature vector ϕ(s)\phi(s)ϕ(s) and weight vector www, define vw(s)=ϕ(s)⊤wv_w(s)=\phi(s)^\top wvw​(s)=ϕ(s)⊤w, where ⊤\top⊤ means transpose. Let δt\delta_tδt​ be the TD error, w+w^+w+ the updated weights and αt\alpha_tαt​ the current step size. St+1S_{t+1}St+1​ is the observed successor:

δt=Rt+1+γvw(St+1)−vw(St),w+=w+αtδtϕ(St).\begin{aligned} \delta_t&=R_{t+1}+\gamma v_w(S_{t+1})-v_w(S_t),\\ w^+&=w+\alpha_t\delta_t\phi(S_t). \end{aligned} δt​w+​=Rt+1​+γvw​(St+1​)−vw​(St​),=w+αt​δt​ϕ(St​).​

For any value vector vvv, let TπvT^\pi vTπv be the expected one-step reward plus discounted next value under π\piπ. Let DDD have stationary state probabilities d(s)d(s)d(s) on its diagonal, with weighted norm for a value vector xxx defined by ∥x∥D2=∑sd(s)x(s)2\|x\|_D^2=\sum_s d(s)x(s)^2∥x∥D2​=∑s​d(s)x(s)2. Let ΠD\Pi_DΠD​ be orthogonal projection onto the feature space in this norm. The squared norm above defines the distance after taking its square root. For candidate value vectors v,uv,uv,u, the composition ΠDTπ\Pi_DT^\piΠD​Tπ first forms the Bellman target and then projects it:

∥ΠDTπv−ΠDTπu∥D≤γ∥v−u∥D.\|\Pi_DT^\pi v-\Pi_DT^\pi u\|_D\leq\gamma\|v-u\|_D. ∥ΠD​Tπv−ΠD​Tπu∥D​≤γ∥v−u∥D​.

Numerical reading: with γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, two candidate predictions at distance 2 in this norm are at most 1.8 apart after the projected map. We measure the distance with the same stationary probabilities before and after. If we change those probabilities, this particular comparison no longer holds.

Stationary averaging and orthogonal projection don't enlarge the distance, and discounting shrinks it. There is one projected fixed point. Under its conditions, sampled linear TD reaches that solution, though its update isn't literally repeated projection. Off-policy state weighting can break the argument because the norms no longer match. Tsitsiklis and Van Roy.

Conditions for this linear prediction result

This is a fixed-policy prediction result. A finite irreducible, aperiodic chain supplies a stationary distribution and repeated on-policy visits. Rewards are bounded, the discount is below 1, and the fixed feature columns are linearly independent.

Positive diminishing learning rates have infinite sum and finite squared sum: they retain enough total adjustment while suppressing persistent sampling noise. These assumptions support the linear result cited above; they do not cover arbitrary neural networks or a changing control policy.

Keep the labels fixed

A moving target prevents us from fitting an ordinary fixed objective. So let's keep approximation and off-policy data, but wait for reward-only returns. With suitable coverage, importance correction can give us target-policy labels without using a guessed future value. We freeze those labels before fitting.

Let XXX be the fixed feature matrix, yyy the vector of corrected labels, and www the linear weights. The Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ measures vector length. Let LLL be squared-error loss and η\etaη the batch learning rate. X⊤X^\topX⊤ transposes XXX, and w+w^+w+ is the updated vector:

L(w)=12∥Xw−y∥22,w+=w−ηX⊤(Xw−y).\begin{aligned} L(w)&=\tfrac12\|Xw-y\|_2^2,\\ w^+&=w-\eta X^\top(Xw-y). \end{aligned} L(w)w+​=21​∥Xw−y∥22​,=w−ηX⊤(Xw−y).​

If XXX has full column rank, its curvature matrix X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X is positive definite. Let λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ be that matrix's largest eigenvalue and w∗w_*w∗​ the unique empirical minimizer. The notation −1^{-1}−1 means inverse:

0<η<2λmax⁡⟹w→w∗=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.0<\eta<\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w\to w_*=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y. 0<η<λmax​2​⟹w→w∗​=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.

One-dimensional check: with X=[1]X=[1]X=[1] and y=[2]y=[2]y=[2], the largest eigenvalue is 1. Let's choose η=0.5\eta=0.5η=0.5, which is within the bound. The update becomes w+=w−0.5(w−2)w^+=w-0.5(w-2)w+=w−0.5(w−2), taking 0→1→1.5→1.750\to1\to1.5\to1.750→1→1.5→1.75. It approaches the fixed label of 2.

With that step size, every curvature direction contracts. If we add bootstrapping, the labels depend on the current predictions, so this fixed-objective argument no longer applies. Sutton and Barto, §§5.5, 9.2.

Conditions for this regression example

Freeze the target and behavior policies, linear features and recorded data. Use independent finite-horizon episodes with bounded rewards and features. Behavior must cover the target actions and the starting states whose values are being fitted; corrected labels need finite variance for statistical claims.

Full column rank gives a unique empirical fit. The batch step-size bound stated above makes optimization approach it. Finite data need not recover the true target-policy value; large importance weights can make that statistical estimate poor.

Separate the table entries

When we fit the current state, a shared weight can also change the successor prediction. Let's keep bootstrapping and off-policy learning, but remove that coupling by giving every state-action pair its own table entry. Let QQQ be that table. The symbols s,a,r,s′s,a,r,s's,a,r,s′ denote the observed St,At,Rt+1,St+1S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1}St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​, and a′a'a′ ranges over next actions. Q-learning changes only:

Q+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+αt[r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)].Q^+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+\alpha_t\bigl[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)\bigr]. Q+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+αt​[r+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)].

One entry at a time: with reward 0, next-row maximum 5 and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, the target is 4.5. A step size of 0.5 takes an old entry of 2 to 3.25. Every other table entry, including the successor maximum, stays unchanged during this update.

Let T∗T_*T∗​ map a candidate table to its expected Q-learning target. For candidate tables q,uq,uq,u, define ∥q−u∥∞\|q-u\|_\infty∥q−u∥∞​ as their largest absolute entrywise difference. The composition T∗qT_*qT∗​q applies that expected-target map to qqq; ≤\leq≤ means at most. Then:

∥T∗q−T∗u∥∞≤γ∥q−u∥∞.\|T_*q-T_*u\|_\infty\leq\gamma\|q-u\|_\infty. ∥T∗​q−T∗​u∥∞​≤γ∥q−u∥∞​.

A maximum and an expectation cannot enlarge the largest difference, and discounting shrinks it. With enough sampling, Q-learning converges to the optimal table. Shared approximation adds a fitting step that can also change the next-state values. Once that happens, the tabular argument alone no longer controls learning. Watkins and Dayan, 1992.

Conditions for tabular Q-learning

The task is a finite Markov decision process with fixed transition and reward laws, bounded rewards and discount below 1. Every nonterminal state-action pair must receive infinitely many updates.

Each pair's positive learning rates are at most 1, have infinite sum and finite squared sum. A replay buffer omitting a pair fails the visit assumption; a constant noisy step size fails the shrinking-step assumption. The theorem cited above concerns the resulting infinite update sequence, not a finite successful route.

Slow the target feedback

The guessed tail can change after every shared-weight update. DQN keeps all three ingredients, so it needs ways to slow that feedback. It uses two devices to help manage it. Replay samples stored transitions, reducing temporal correlation and changing the update distribution. A frozen target network holds the guessed labels still for a bounded period. Replay doesn't make the data on-policy.

Let QθQ_\thetaQθ​ be the online action-value network with weights θ\thetaθ, and Qθ−Q_{\theta^-}Qθ−​ its frozen copy. Let ddd be one for a terminal transition and zero otherwise, yyy the target, and ∇θ\nabla_\theta∇θ​ the gradient with respect to online weights. Here s,a,r,s′s,a,r,s's,a,r,s′ are the current state, action, observed reward and successor. The symbol a′a'a′ ranges over next actions, and θ+\theta^+θ+ is the updated online network. The superscript minus labels the frozen copy, not subtraction. Using these transition symbols:

y=r+γ(1−d)max⁡a′Qθ−(s′,a′),θ+=θ+αt[y−Qθ(s,a)]∇θQθ(s,a).\begin{aligned} y&=r+\gamma(1-d)\max_{a'}Q_{\theta^-}(s',a'),\\ \theta^+&=\theta+\alpha_t[y-Q_\theta(s,a)]\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s,a). \end{aligned} yθ+​=r+γ(1−d)a′max​Qθ−​(s′,a′),=θ+αt​[y−Qθ​(s,a)]∇θ​Qθ​(s,a).​

The terminal mask removes the nonexistent future after an episode ends. This is a semi-gradient update: gradients flow through the current prediction while yyy stays fixed. Let CCC be the positive number of updates between target copies:

store each observed transition in replay
sample a transition (s, a, r, s′, d)
compute y using frozen weights theta_minus
update online weights theta toward y
if C updates have passed: theta_minus = theta

Freezing delays the target feedback, but it doesn't prove global convergence, even in the two-state family of examples. Mnih et al., Methods, primary PDF; van Hasselt et al..

Check estimates beside rewards

A task score tells you how the policy acts. Value estimates also need checking. If each reward has absolute magnitude at most Rmax⁡R_{\max}Rmax​, let GtG_tGt​ be the discounted return from step ttt. The bars ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ mean absolute magnitude. The return adds future rewards with a factor γ\gammaγ per step; the geometric sum gives:

∣Gt∣≤Rmax⁡1−γ.|G_t|\leq\frac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}. ∣Gt​∣≤1−γRmax​​.

For example, if rewards are bounded in magnitude by 1 and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, the bound is 10. A prediction of 100 cannot be the correct discounted return. Start by checking the reward scale and terminal handling, then inspect sampling and target feedback.

An estimate outside this range is wrong for the specified discounted task. A finite spike establishes an error, but claiming divergence to infinity is a stronger mathematical statement.

  • Coverage: identify which states and actions the updates omit.
  • Coupling: check which other predictions move after one update.
  • Targets: identify when labels change and where gradients stop.
  • Scope: linear prediction and tabular convergence results require their stated conditions.
The three pairs: detailed stability arguments and conditions

Each pair below has a particular stable construction under stated assumptions. They explain why removing one source of feedback can help. The deadly triad names a risk when all three ingredients are present; it is not a rule that every pair is safe or every triple diverges.

In the equations below, ttt is the time step; StS_tSt​ and AtA_tAt​ are the state and action; Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ is the next reward. The target policy π(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s)π(a∣s) gives the probability of action aaa in state sss; b(a∣s)b(a\mid s)b(a∣s) is the policy that collected the data. The discount is 0≤γ<10\leq\gamma<10≤γ<1 and αt>0\alpha_t>0αt​>0 is a learning step size. A superscript +++ means the next parameter or table value.

1 · Approximation + bootstrapping

Learn a fixed policy's values with on-policy linear TD. A fixed feature vector ϕ(s)\phi(s)ϕ(s) describes state sss; the weights www produce vw(s)=ϕ(s)⊤wv_w(s)=\phi(s)^\top wvw​(s)=ϕ(s)⊤w. The superscript ⊤\top⊤ means transpose. Let δt\delta_tδt​ be the TD error, and let w+w^+w+ denote the updated weights. One observed transition gives this update:

δt=Rt+1+γvw(St+1)−vw(St),w+=w+αtδtϕ(St).\begin{aligned} \delta_t &= R_{t+1}+\gamma v_w(S_{t+1})-v_w(S_t),\\ w^+ &= w+\alpha_t\delta_t\phi(S_t). \end{aligned} δt​w+​=Rt+1​+γvw​(St+1​)−vw​(St​),=w+αt​δt​ϕ(St​).​

Why can this settle down? For a candidate value vector vvv, let TπT^\piTπ be the Bellman prediction operator:

(Tπv)(s)=Eπ[Rt+1+γv(St+1)∣St=s].(T^\pi v)(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[ R_{t+1}+\gamma v(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s]. (Tπv)(s)=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γv(St+1​)∣St​=s].

The expectation uses the fixed target policy and the environment's transition probabilities. Let DDD put its stationary state probabilities d(s)d(s)d(s) on the diagonal; ∥x∥D2=∑sd(s)x(s)2\|x\|_D^2=\sum_s d(s)x(s)^2∥x∥D2​=∑s​d(s)x(s)2 weights a value vector xxx by those probabilities. Let Π\PiΠ be least-squares projection onto the space spanned by the fixed features, using those same weights. For value vectors vvv and uuu:

∥ΠTπv−ΠTπu∥D≤γ∥v−u∥D.\|\Pi T^\pi v-\Pi T^\pi u\|_D \leq\gamma\|v-u\|_D. ∥ΠTπv−ΠTπu∥D​≤γ∥v−u∥D​.

On-policy averaging cannot enlarge this norm; neither can the orthogonal projection. Multiplying by γ<1\gamma<1γ<1 makes the combined map a contraction, with one projected fixed point v=ΠTπvv=\Pi T^\pi vv=ΠTπv. TD's sampled weight update is not literally repeated projection. Under the conditions below, it converges to that same projected solution. Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, Sections IV and VII.

Add off-policy sampling: projection may now weight states by the behavior distribution, while the Bellman target follows π\piπ. The matched-norm argument can fail. The two-state example earlier in this article shows the resulting feedback.

Read the bound: if two candidate value vectors are distance 2 apart and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, one projected Bellman map leaves them at most 1.8 apart. It compares two whole predictions under the same policy and state weighting. It does not say every noisy TD sample improves its estimate.

Conditions behind this prediction result

This is a fixed-policy prediction result. A finite irreducible, aperiodic chain supplies a stationary distribution and repeated on-policy visits. Rewards are bounded, the discount is below 1, and the fixed feature columns are linearly independent.

Positive diminishing learning rates have infinite sum and finite squared sum: they retain enough total adjustment while suppressing persistent sampling noise. These assumptions support the linear result cited above; they do not cover arbitrary neural networks or a changing control policy.

2 · Approximation + off-policy

Wait for the complete return, then fit fixed targets. Let HHH be the terminal time, kkk index future steps, GtG_tGt​ be the full discounted return and ρt\rho_tρt​ be the trajectory weight correcting behavior bbb to target policy π\piπ. The product ∏\prod∏ multiplies the action-probability ratios along that recorded future. Its return and importance weight are

Gt=∑k=0H−t−1γkRt+k+1,ρt=∏k=tH−1π(Ak∣Sk)b(Ak∣Sk).\begin{aligned} G_t &= \sum_{k=0}^{H-t-1}\gamma^k R_{t+k+1},\\ \rho_t &= \prod_{k=t}^{H-1} \frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{b(A_k\mid S_k)}. \end{aligned} Gt​ρt​​=k=0∑H−t−1​γkRt+k+1​,=k=t∏H−1​b(Ak​∣Sk​)π(Ak​∣Sk​)​.​

Crucially, GtG_tGt​ contains rewards, not a guessed future value. Freeze the recorded data. For example iii, use its corrected return yi=ρiGiy_i=\rho_i G_iyi​=ρi​Gi​ as the label; here GiG_iGi​ and ρi\rho_iρi​ mean the return and weight for that recorded starting point. Let yyy stack these labels, and let row iii of the feature matrix XXX be ϕ(si)⊤\phi(s_i)^\topϕ(si​)⊤, with sis_isi​ the example's starting state. Let η>0\eta>0η>0 be the batch step size; X⊤X^\topX⊤ is the transposed feature matrix. Batch gradient descent is

w+=w−ηX⊤(Xw−y).w^+=w-\eta X^\top(Xw-y). w+=w−ηX⊤(Xw−y).

The Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ measures vector length. The fixed squared-error loss is L(w)=12∥Xw−y∥22L(w)=\tfrac12\|Xw-y\|_2^2L(w)=21​∥Xw−y∥22​. Let w∗w_*w∗​ be its empirical minimizer, ≻0\succ0≻0 mean positive definite, and −1^{-1}−1 mean matrix inverse. If XXX has full column rank,

X⊤X≻0⟹w∗=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.X^\top X\succ0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad w_*=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y. X⊤X≻0⟹w∗​=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.

Full rank gives one empirical least-squares minimizer. Choose η\etaη below 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue of X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X: then the error in each curvature direction shrinks. The labels stay fixed while the weights move. Rank-deficient data need not have a unique fit. This is a well-posed regression argument, not a blanket convergence claim for off-policy Monte Carlo. Sutton and Barto, published second edition, §§5.5 and 9.2.

Add bootstrapping: replace the complete return with a target containing vwv_wvw​ at a future state. Now the labels move with www. Treating them as constants during each update no longer gives gradient descent on the fixed regression above.

One fixed label: take one feature equal to 1 and a corrected return label of 2. The loss is (w−2)2/2(w-2)^2/2(w−2)2/2. With batch step size η=0.5\eta=0.5η=0.5, weights 0,1,1.5,1.750,1,1.5,1.750,1,1.5,1.75 approach 2 because the label stays 2. Bootstrapping would let that destination move with the predictions.

Conditions behind this regression example

Freeze the target and behavior policies, linear features and recorded data. Use independent finite-horizon episodes with bounded rewards and features. Behavior must cover the target actions and the starting states whose values are being fitted; corrected labels need finite variance for statistical claims.

Full column rank gives a unique empirical fit. The batch step-size bound stated above makes optimization approach it. Finite data need not recover the true target-policy value; large importance weights can make that statistical estimate poor.

3 · Bootstrapping + off-policy

Keep a separate table entry for every state-action pair. Let QQQ be the action-value table. In a transition (s,a,r,s′)(s,a,r,s')(s,a,r,s′), sss and aaa are the state and action, rrr the reward and s′s's′ the next state; a′a'a′ ranges over next actions. Tabular Q-learning updates just one entry:

Q+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+αt[r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)].\begin{aligned} Q^+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+\alpha_t\big[&r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\\ &-Q(s,a)\big]. \end{aligned} Q+(s,a)=Q(s,a)+αt​[​r+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)].​

All other entries stay unchanged. For any candidate table qqq, its expected target is the Bellman optimality operator T∗T_*T∗​:

(T∗q)(s,a)=E ⁣[r+γmax⁡a′q(s′,a′)∣s,a].(T_*q)(s,a)=\mathbb E\!\left[ r+\gamma\max_{a'}q(s',a')\mid s,a\right]. (T∗​q)(s,a)=E[r+γa′max​q(s′,a′)∣s,a].

The expectation averages the environment's rewards and transitions. The max norm ∥x∥∞=max⁡s,a∣x(s,a)∣\|x\|_\infty=\max_{s,a}|x(s,a)|∥x∥∞​=maxs,a​∣x(s,a)∣ is the largest absolute entry of a table xxx. For two candidate tables qqq and uuu,

∥T∗q−T∗u∥∞≤γ∥q−u∥∞.\|T_*q-T_*u\|_\infty \leq\gamma\|q-u\|_\infty. ∥T∗​q−T∗​u∥∞​≤γ∥q−u∥∞​.

Taking a maximum and averaging cannot amplify the largest entrywise difference; discounting shrinks it. Thus T∗T_*T∗​ has one fixed point, the optimal table. With enough visits and suitable step sizes, sampled Q-learning reaches it. Watkins and Dayan's convergence theorem.

Add function approximation: a weight update can also change other states' values, including a value in the bootstrap target. The tabular Bellman operator still contracts, but that alone does not control the added shared fitting step. Its guarantee does not transfer to an arbitrary approximator.

Two separate entries: if the successor maximum is 5, the reward is 0 and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, the target is 4.5. Moving a predecessor from 2 toward 4.5 leaves the successor at 5 during that update. A shared weight can move both; a table entry cannot.

Conditions behind tabular convergence

The task is a finite Markov decision process with fixed transition and reward laws, bounded rewards and discount below 1. Every nonterminal state-action pair must receive infinitely many updates.

Each pair's positive learning rates are at most 1, have infinite sum and finite squared sum. A replay buffer omitting a pair fails the visit assumption; a constant noisy step size fails the shrinking-step assumption. The theorem cited above concerns the resulting infinite update sequence, not a finite successful route.

Across the series, we've used values to connect late rewards to earlier choices. The triad matters because sharing that credit can also share an error, which then becomes the next target. Return to the method tree, or the opening problems.

The next three parts look at failures outside the triad: policy-gradient credit and update size, learning from a fixed dataset, and mode averaging. The failure map groups them all.
